## The Tense-Aspect Matrix

English does not merely indicate *when* an event occurs (tense: Past, Present, Future). It communicates *how* that event unfolds in time (aspect: Simple, Progressive/Continuous, Perfect, Perfect Continuous). 

Together, these form a $3 \times 4$ grid of twelve distinct temporal states:

| Tense / Aspect | Simple | Continuous (Progressive) | Perfect | Perfect Continuous |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Present** | *I write* (habitual/fact) | *I am writing* (ongoing) | *I have written* (completed with present relevance) | *I have been writing* (duration leading to now) |
| **Past** | *I wrote* (completed past) | *I was writing* (interrupted past) | *I had written* (past prior to another past) | *I had been writing* (past duration prior to past event) |
| **Future** | *I will write* (volition/prediction) | *I will be writing* (ongoing future) | *I will have written* (completion before future marker) | *I will have been writing* (ongoing duration until future point) |

## Semantic Nuances

### 1. The Perfect Aspect ($Have + V_{3}$)
The perfect aspect connects two distinct temporal frames. The present perfect (*"She has completed the proof"*) indicates that an event occurred in an unspecified past, but its consequence dictates current reality.

### 2. The Stative Constraint
Verbs of cognition, emotion, and possession (*know, believe, belong, love*) resist progressive aspects in standard English. Saying *"I am knowing the answer"* violates the aspectual boundary of stative verbs.
